explanation: Most screenings had live music, from a lone pianist to a full orchestra. In Japan, narrators called benshi also stood beside the screen and voiced the story.

claims.text: Most silent films were shown with live musical accompaniment rather than in silence.
Accompaniment ranged from a single pianist or organist to a full orchestra.
In Japan, live narrators called benshi stood beside the screen and voiced the story of silent films.

writerNotes: Self-check 9.3. Lint: clean. Claims: every claim listed, risk at or above the C26 floor and raised where a detail is easy to get wrong; the schema's riskReason list has no 'only' or 'counterintuitive', so such claims carry the nearest listed reason. Datasets: no pinned dataset covers film or TV facts, so every high-risk claim here needs checker evidence from the web. Rival test: Arguing for the statement: the films themselves had no recorded sound, which is why the belief is common; but screenings almost always had live music or narration. Volatility: evergreen; no time words; nothing depends on events after mid-2026. Regional: silent cinema was shown the same way worldwide, and the Japanese benshi example widens it beyond Europe and the US. Style: Oxford spelling, straight single quotes, plain hyphens, explanation of 27 words. Myths: claims screened against myths.json; no claim resembles a listed myth. Mystery and encore: not applicable to a practice item. Doubts: none beyond the high-risk claims flagged for external evidence.

evidence.restatement: Silent films were nearly always screened with live music, so showings in complete silence were the exception.
